extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature interested in questions of truth, style, and purpose in fiction
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-length set of critical claims about what fiction should do — whether stories ought to be true, how they should treat character, pathos, style, and the purposes of literature (escapist vs. revealing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of literature — amusement vs. instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: If literature is to be regarded solely as the amusement of an idle hour, then the less relationship it has to life the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts purely escapist stories (fairyland where virtue always triumphs) with literature that calls us to ponder existence. The implication: be explicit about your aim — if the work is intended purely for entertainment, distance from life is acceptable; if it intends to instruct or help, it should engage with real life and its problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should show life — deal with ugly and beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: If literature is to be a help to us, as well as a pastime, it must deal with the ugly as well as with the beautiful; it must show us ourselves, not as we wish to appear, but as we know ourselves to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Hamlet and Coriolanus as works that provoke thought; Dickens and Zola both having a place. The criterion endorses truthful representation (including uncomfortable truths) when the work aims to be morally or intellectually useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both branches of literature are needful (escapist and realistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are not both branches of literature needful?... By all means let us dream, on midsummer nights, of fond lovers ... But may we not also ... find satisfaction in thinking with Hamlet or Coriolanus?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges tolerance and balance: fairy tales and idealized stories have value for escape, while serious, realistic works have value for reflection; neither alone suffices for all purposes or readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain tale, simply told — longevity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To sum up, 'David Copperfield' is a plain tale, simply told; and such are all books that live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eccentric stylistic devices may please transient critics, but simple, straightforward storytelling is presented as the quality that gives a work lasting life and broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive eccentricities of style / artistic trickery
rubrics_metrics.description: Eccentricities of style, artistic trickery, may please the critic of a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such devices are described as likely ephemeral in value; the guidance is to prioritize clarity and engaging story over showy stylistic effects that risk dating a work or narrowing its readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of literature — reveal rather than flatter
rubrics_metrics.description: Is literature to flatter him, or reveal him to himself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rhetorical question frames a standard: literature that seeks to reveal uncomfortable truths about human nature is more valuable (for the author’s purposes here) than literature that simply flatters readers’ self-images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos: prefer understatement; avoid bathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Too often his pathos sinks to bathos, and this not from want of skill, but from want of care... The death of Barkis ... There is no straining after effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective emotional scenes are understated and earned rather than overwrought. The author contrasts successful modest pathos (Barkis, Colonel Newcome) with sentimental excesses (Little Nell, Paul Dombey) as an anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation: types vs fully individuated characters
rubrics_metrics.description: In Uriah Heap and Mrs. Gummidge, Dickens draws types rather than characters... Pecksniff, Podsnap, Dolly Varden... these are not characters; they are human characteristics personified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that 'types' (personified characteristics) are a legitimate method and often effective, but implies a trade-off: types simplify and amplify certain qualities at the cost of psychological realism. Authors should be aware of this choice and its effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial virtues can compensate for faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are not made worth reading by the absence of absurdities. Ouida possesses strength, tenderness, truth, passion; and these be qualities in a writer capable of carrying many more faults than Ouida is burdened with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of fundamental literary virtues (strength, tenderness, truth, passion) can outweigh technical or factual absurdities. Critics who fixate on minor faults risk missing the larger merits of a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to life is not sufficient for popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: If faithfulness to life were the key to literary success, Gissing’s sales would have been counted by the million instead of by the hundred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism or strict fidelity to life does not automatically attract a wide readership; other qualities (tone, appeal, narrative skill) matter for popular success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of humour and seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Mark Twain’s literary qualities, apart altogether from his humour, been recognised?... 'Huck Finn' would be a great work were there not a laugh in it from cover to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour can coexist with (and even enhance) serious literary achievement; comedic elements do not preclude depth. Authors should note that humour need not reduce literary worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should interest broad audiences (universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature is a story that interests us, boys and girls, men and women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author values works that appeal across ages and demographics; universality of human interest is presented as a hallmark of enduring fiction.
